newsitem.title: GREECE: Albanian premier in Athens to discuss aid force.
newsitem.headline: Albanian premier in Athens to discuss aid force.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino arrived in Athens on Wednesday for talks on his troubled Balkan nation with Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis and envoys from the Organisation for European Security and Cooperation (OSCE) and the European Union.

Fino, 34, appointed to head a unity government after an armed revolt in southern Albania, was expected to discuss a U.N.-approved force to help restore order in his chaotic country and financial aid to cope with an economic crisis.

"Greece will continue to play an important role in normalising the situation in Albania within the framework of international initiatives," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters when asked about the Fino visit.
He said Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo and former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky, special OSCE envoy for Albania, would meet Fino and Greek political leaders on Thursday.
"A quadrilateral meeting will take place," Reppas said. "There is no specific proposal on the table; the agenda is open."
Both the Vienna-based OSCE's envoy Vranitzky and the EU's foreign policy representative, Van Mierlo, were coming to Athens on their own initiative, he added.
Foreign ministry officials said the Italian-led force of about 5,000 men, which Rome says could start deployment by about April 10, would undoubtedly top the agenda.
Designed to secure the distribution of much-needed humanitarian aid in the impoverished country, it will try to secure the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport.
So far Italy is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400.
Greece, gravely concerned with the crisis at its northern border, has also pledged a favourable $75 million loan to Albania as soon as order was restored.
Athens has been closely monitoring the effects of last month's insurrection on the large Greek minority living in the south after much of the area fell to rebel hands.
It is also worried violence and economic disaster in the former communist state could send a new wave of illegal Albanian immigrants through its rugged borderline.
Hundreds of thousands of illegal foreign workers, mostly the result of an Albanian refugee influx after the fall of communism in 1990, are already taxing its fragile economy.

Prompted by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes which left thousands destitute, the revolt has left the south lawless for weeks, with groups armed with weapons looted from army depots roaming the area.

Rebel committees controlling southern towns say they are trying to stop the banditry and looting that has killed scores of people but demand the resignation of President Sali Berisha, blaming him for collapse of the investment schemes.
Berisha has refused to step down but was forced to appoint Fino a socialist, to head a 10-party unity government until elections, expected in June.
